newsitem.title: yugoslavia: Turmoil reigns in Serbian political scene.
newsitem.headline: Turmoil reigns in Serbian political scene.

text.p: Huge street protests over annulled elections have forced President Slobodan Milosevic into making concessions and caused an upheaval in the main governing parties, threatening to transform Serbia's political landscape.
Election commissions in Belgrade and Serbia's second largest city Nis awarded victory to the opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) on Tuesday after almost two months of controversy.
The apparently conciliatory act was welcomed by Zajedno and the West with caution and Belgrade's political establishment warned on Wednesday against premature euphoria over the rulings.
Just before he was sacked, the chief of Belgrade's Socialists, Branislav Ivkovic, said his party would appeal against the commission ruling. It had 48 hours to do so.
Senior political sources warned that timing was crucial as even Socialist diehards were wary of whipping up the wrath of the West on which Serbia must depend for economic aid.

In an illustration of the cat-and-mouse game it was playing against the opposition and the West, the Belgrade SPS later said it had still not officially received the commission decision, even though more than 24 hours had expired, extending the deadline for appeals.
Political sources said the electoral commissions had ruled on the initiative of the small New Democracy Party.
The party is allied to Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS) and the Yugoslav United Left (JUL) of his wife Mira Markovic.
JUL spokesman Aleksandar Vulin defended the ruling, saying the electoral commissioners acted in keeping with the law.

"New Democracy is trying to save President Milosevic from himself and his hardline associates," a senior political source explained, noting that New Democracy had called for the restoration of Zajedno's victory all along.
"Now the JUL is jumping on the bandwagon, making it appear that it favoured the rule of law all along, leaving hardline SPS members to hold the soiled end of the stick," he said.

Zajedno won control of 14 large towns including Belgrade in municipal elections last November but the results were annulled. The move provoked more than eight weeks of street protests by the opposition.
Analysts said the outcome was far from certain despite a Serbian government promise to protesting Belgrade students that their demands would be met.
The students' agenda is similar to that of Zajedno -- restoration of opposition victories, punishment of those accused of forging election results and free access to the media.
The students were also demanding the replacement of the rector of Belgrade University, a Socialist.
The Socialist-dominated Belgrade University Council on Wednesday voted to keep the rector in his post, indicating the diehards were gaining the upper hand.
Council's deputy chairman Vlajko Brajic, a professor at the Belgrade Law Faculty, submitted his resignation because, as he said, "he was told how to vote."
The Socialist leadership sacked Mile Ilic, the party's hardline chief in Nis, on Tuesday. It also removed the moderate Mayor of Belgrade, Nebojsa Covic, balancing the score.
It replaced Ivkovic, but with another hardliner -- Dragan Tomic, the speaker of the Serbian parliament who gained notoriety when he called the street protesters "fascists".
New Democracy has now threatened to walk out of the leftist alliance.

Milosevic and Markovic have not made any public statements on the situation to provide any guidance to their supporters. But analysts said New Democracy's moves were providing them with a way out of the crisis.
"The emperor has neither given the thumbs up nor thumbs down sign but by the time the arena closes there will a lot of casualties in the field," the political source said.
